title: Everyone talks of bliss
hookLine: everyone speaks of bliss, but bliss is known through the Guru (Anand 6)

cards: Search happiness in any bookstore and you'll get a wall. Ten steps to joy. The happiness project.
Happy in thirty days. Apps that track your mood. Podcasts promising bliss by Friday.
Everybody's talking about it, and somehow the people talking most aren't always the ones who seem to have it.
The sixth pauri of Anand Sahib noticed the same thing, long before the first self-help shelf, with an opening that could have been written this morning.

teach.b: The line: anand anand sabh ko kahai, anand guroo te jaaniaa.
Everyone speaks of bliss, bliss; but bliss is known through the Guru. Then, in paraphrase: true bliss is always known through the Guru, when the Beloved shows grace.

By grace, wrongdoings are cut away, and the ointment of spiritual wisdom is put on the eyes. Those whose attachment has broken from within are made beautiful by the true Word. Says Nanak, this is bliss.

teach.h: GIAAN ANJAN: WISDOM ON THE EYES.
teach.b: Stop on the image in the middle: giaan anjan, the ointment of wisdom. Anjan is the dark ointment people lined their eyes with. So wisdom here isn't more information.
It's something applied to your eyes, so you see differently. The world doesn't change; your sight does.
Then the key phrase: those whose attachment, moh, has broken from within.

That's the difference between the talk and the real thing. Much of the bliss on that bookstore wall is a new thing to grab: a purchase, a trip, a win. The pauri's bliss starts with letting go of the grabbing.
It's received by grace and recognized from inside, not bought or argued into. And the word is jaaniaa, known: not felt for an afternoon, known the way you know your own front door.
Sikhs don't say ordinary happiness is bad; a good meal, a good laugh, are gifts. The pauri just points to a deeper joy, and some readers put it simply: it doesn't leave when the afternoon does.

how: Many Sikhs recite this sixth pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem; its opening line is often quoted in Sikh teaching about the difference between pleasure and true bliss.

o: wisdom's ointment, so the eyes see anew
dark eyeliner worn for a wedding day
a book of wisdom read every morning

p: the ointment of wisdom on the eyes

s: pauri six says ordinary happiness is bad
it says there's a deeper joy, known through the Guru, that doesn't leave when the afternoon does.
the pauri pictures wisdom as an ointment put on the eyes
giaan anjan: the world doesn't change, your sight does.
pauri six is one of the six sung at every service's close
the short form is pauris one to five and forty; pauri six is in the full forty.

games.q: everyone around you is talking about bliss, and selling it too. what does pauri six say about where it's known?
o: bliss is known through the Guru.
games.why: anand anand sabh ko kahai, anand guroo te jaaniaa: everyone speaks of bliss; bliss is known through the Guru, when attachment breaks within.

practice: Think back to a moment of real joy, not excitement or a win but the quieter kind that stayed: holding a newborn, a moment in prayer, a long talk, a sunrise you didn't expect.
Let it come back, notice where you feel it in the body, and notice what you weren't grabbing for. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you hold it; if not, just remember.

carryVoice: Your line: real joy. It starts where the grip loosens, not where it tightens. See you tomorrow.
